prompt: In Cleveland and McGill's experiments, which channel did people judge most accurately?

choices.text: Position on a common scale
choices.why: Right. Two dots or two bar ends against one axis gave the smallest errors.

choices.text: Area
choices.why: Area was near the bottom, above only volume and shading.

choices.text: Angle
choices.why: Angle sat in the middle, with length and direction.

choices.text: Colour saturation, from pale to vivid
choices.why: Saturation came last of all.

prompt: Put these channels in Cleveland and McGill's order, from most to least accurately judged.
trap: Two dots on separate scales still beat any angle.

prompt: What did the experiments ask people to judge?

choices.text: Which of the two marks they preferred
choices.why: Preference was not measured. Accuracy was.

choices.text: How quickly they could find the larger mark
choices.why: Speed is a separate question. The experiments compared the answers with the true ratios.

choices.text: Which chart type was most attractive
choices.why: Nothing about attractiveness was asked; that is why the result is not a matter of taste.

choices.text: What percentage the smaller mark was of the larger
choices.why: Right. The ratio between two marks is what a reader of a chart is always estimating.

prompt: On a map of Brazil's states, why can the number of orders not go into position, the best channel?

choices.text: Geography already uses it
choices.why: Right. Geography takes both positions, so the number goes down the ladder, into colour or area.

choices.text: Maps cannot show numbers
choices.why: They can, through colour, symbols or labels, just not through position.

choices.text: Position is only accurate for bar charts
choices.why: Position is the most accurate channel in any chart that has it free.

choices.text: The states are too different in size
choices.why: That is a real problem for choropleth maps, but it is not why position is unavailable.

prompt: A pie chart encodes each value in which two channels?

choices.text: Angle and area
choices.why: Right. Both sit low on the ladder, which is the pie's problem.

choices.text: Length and position
choices.why: Those are a bar chart's channels.

choices.text: Hue and shape together
choices.why: The colours of a pie separate slices; they carry no amount.

choices.text: Position and colour
choices.why: A slice's position round the circle carries no amount either.

prompt: Dairy earned R$ 351 thousand and Pantry R$ 239 thousand. By what percentage did Dairy beat Pantry? Answer to the nearest whole number.
Somebody prints the percentage on every slice of a six-slice pie. What does that tell you about the chart?

choices.text: The chart is now as good as a bar chart
choices.why: The reader can now get the answer, but by reading, not by looking.

choices.text: The slices were drawn at the wrong angles
choices.why: The angles can be perfect. The eye is what reads them badly.

choices.text: Pies need percentages by law in published reports
choices.why: There is no such rule.

choices.text: The numbers are doing the work the picture could not
choices.why: Right. A pie that needs its numbers is a table drawn in a circle.

prompt: Why does a 3D pie mislead even when every slice has the correct angle?

choices.text: It uses more colours
choices.why: It uses the same colours. The distortion is in the shapes.

choices.text: The front slices are drawn larger
choices.why: Right. The same number takes up more of the picture in front.

choices.text: 3D charts are slower to draw
choices.why: Speed is not a matter of honesty.

choices.text: It leaves out the smallest slices to make room for the depth
choices.why: A 3D pie still draws every slice, just at the wrong apparent size.

prompt: According to Stevens's power law, why do big circles look smaller than they are, relative to small ones?

choices.text: The exponent for area is above 1
choices.why: An exponent above 1 would make big areas look bigger, the opposite of what was measured.

choices.text: The exponent for area is below 1
choices.why: Right. Raised to about 0.7, a big ratio comes out much smaller.

choices.text: Circles are always drawn by radius
choices.why: Drawing by radius would exaggerate them. The effect here is in the eye.

choices.text: Screens shrink large shapes more than small ones
choices.why: Nothing shrinks on the screen. The perception is what compresses.

prompt: With an exponent of 0.7 for area, how many times larger does a circle with 10 times the area appear? Answer to one decimal place.
hint: Raise the real ratio to the exponent.

prompt: Which response to the area problem does the lesson argue against?

choices.text: Preferring length or position when the comparison matters
choices.why: That is the first response the lesson recommends.

choices.text: Labelling the values that matter on an area chart
choices.why: The lesson recommends this, so the reader does not have to judge the areas.

choices.text: Sizing the marks by area rather than by radius
choices.why: That is the honest way to size them, and the lesson asks for it.

choices.text: Inflating the big symbols
choices.why: Right. It fixes the average reader and misleads the one who measures, and the exponent varies by person.

prompt: A bubble chart shows revenue as circle area, and the largest bubble is twice the next. How will most readers see the difference?

choices.text: Exactly double
choices.why: Only a channel with an exponent of 1, such as length, reads true.

choices.text: Larger than double: about 2.6 times
choices.why: That would need an exponent above 1. Area's is below.

choices.text: Smaller than double: about 1.6 times
choices.why: Right. Two raised to 0.7 is about 1.62.

choices.text: Four times as large
choices.why: Four times is what doubling the radius produces in area, not how a doubled area looks.

prompt: What job does a pie do well?

choices.text: Comparing many categories that are close in size
choices.why: That is exactly where angles fail and bars succeed.

choices.text: Showing one part against its whole
choices.why: Right. The circle itself says the slices add up to 100%.

choices.text: Showing change over time
choices.why: Change over time belongs on a line, with time along the horizontal.

choices.text: Comparing two years side by side
choices.why: Two pies side by side is the worst use the lesson names.

prompt: If you have to draw a pie, which of these does the lesson ask for? Choose every one that applies.

choices.text: Tilt it into 3D so it looks more finished
choices.why: 3D draws the front slices larger than the back ones.

choices.text: Sort the slices from the largest, starting at twelve o'clock
choices.why: Right. It gives the circle a start the reader can find.

choices.text: Merge everything past the fifth slice into other
choices.why: Right. Five slices at most.

choices.text: Label the slices directly instead of with a legend
choices.why: Right. Matching colours to a legend is work the reader should not have to do.

choices.text: Pull the slices apart so each one is easy to see
choices.why: An exploded pie removes the shared edges the eye uses.

prompt: Two pies, one for 2024 and one for 2025, sit side by side to show how the categories changed. What would serve the reader better?

choices.text: A larger pie for the year with more revenue
choices.why: That adds an area comparison on top of two angle comparisons.

choices.text: The same two pies, with percentages printed on the slices
choices.why: Then the reader compares numbers, not the chart.

choices.text: A stacked bar for each year, or a line per category
choices.why: Right. Both replace two sets of angles with position and length.

choices.text: Two donut charts instead
choices.why: A donut is judged by arc length, which is no better than angle.

prompt: Which pie is most likely to be read correctly?

choices.text: Six slices between 12% and 21%
choices.why: Close values in many slices is the pie's worst case.

choices.text: Four slices of 24%, 25%, 25% and 26%
choices.why: Nobody can see a one-point difference in an angle.

choices.text: Eight slices sorted by size
choices.why: Sorting helps, but eight slices is too many.

choices.text: Two slices, 26% and 74%
choices.why: Right. Two slices, and one near a quarter, a landmark the eye judges well.

prompt: In pie.py, why is the data sorted before either chart is drawn?

choices.text: So both charts share one order
choices.why: Right. A fair comparison changes only the channel, not the order.

choices.text: matplotlib refuses unsorted data for a pie
choices.why: It draws whatever order it is given.

choices.text: To remove the smallest category
choices.why: All six are kept.

choices.text: Sorting is what computes the percentages
choices.why: The percentages come from dividing by the total, in a separate line.

prompt: Match each chart to the channel that carries its numbers.
Cleveland and McGill's 1984 paper was called Graphical ___.
A report shows a donut with the total revenue printed in its hole. A colleague says the donut is better than a pie because of that total. What does the lesson say?

choices.text: The donut is read more accurately because there is no centre angle
choices.why: Without the angle the reader judges arc length, which is no better.

choices.text: The donut is worse than a pie in every respect
choices.why: It has the advantage of room for a total.

choices.text: The total is its only gain, and a bar chart carries it too
choices.why: Right. The donut makes room for a number but reads its slices no better.

choices.text: A total should not be shown with a part-to-whole chart
choices.why: Showing the whole beside the parts is reasonable.

prompt: Horta's six categories earned 1,960 thousand reais in total and Vegetables earned 412. What share is that, as a percentage to one decimal place?
